chapter: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
title: Funeral music, the marshal and John Casimir's tears
summary: Funeral bands switched from fast warm-up numbers to slow marches, the marshal set the mood, and Casimir wept while playing clarinet.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: But that was always a striking and exciting thing is when at a funeral, and I really didn't go to a lot of funerals, maybe three or four, maybe a couple more, but that they would play that, the band and the club that was the deceased had been a member of, they would assemble somewhere a couple of blocks away and then they would have this warm-up fast number and kind of get right and then get over to the home or the funeral parlor and when they finally brought the casket out then they would go to the church where they want to preach over them and they would play the slow, durage numbers. And they would play the same number sometimes in this March, dead March time as opposed to the fast, happy warm-up time and just change the whole mood of the whole occasion. just in an instant. And the marshal, the person who was the member of the club who was leading the parade and who set the tone of it a lot by his own sort of step and demeanor. also could just change the tone of it just by changing the way he held himself and the way he did his steps going down the street. he had control of that. It was rather remarkable. I always thought that the mood of it could be changed and become very sad ensemble. John Casimir, when he would play for those funeral parades, I've seen him on, I perhaps shouldn't say many occasions, but certainly on more than one occasion when he would be playing the slow marches when they were going to the church or from the church to the cemetery, would become so involved in the music that he would have tears just streaming down his cheeks while he was playing his clarinet. And he was not involved in the occasion. He was just, you know, they were there playing for the occasion. But he just, he got himself so caught up in the emotional power of the music that he, the tears are just streaming down his cheeks while he was playing his horn. And I always found that to be very powerful and very moving, that he would do that. Getting close to the end of your tape.
